HIST 101 · Chapter 11 · Lecture 3

Removal

The Cherokee Nation, the Trail of Tears, and the question of ethnic cleansing

Georgia to Indian Territory · 1828–1839

Background: AI-generated historical interpretation of a Cherokee family on the road west, 1838 (1830s American oil-painting style); not a surviving historical image

Today's lecture tells one story from beginning to end: how the Cherokee Nation lost its homeland in the 1830s. Then, and only then, it gives you a tool for judging that story.

Keep one sentence in mind the whole way through: the Cherokee answered removal with every peaceful tool a republic is supposed to honor, a written constitution, a newspaper, petitions, and a Supreme Court victory, and the United States removed them anyway, first by law and then by force.

The Cherokee were not alone. The Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, and Seminole were removed in the same decade, and you will meet them briefly today and more fully in the Pierian Spring section at the end.

Look at the background. It is an AI-generated interpretation, not a picture from 1838: a family walking beside an ox wagon, soldiers on the road behind them. Hold that image; the lecture will explain how they got onto that road.

At the end, you will learn the definition your Ethnic Cleansing capstone uses, because right after this lecture you start applying it to this very case.

Check yourself: What do you already think the phrase "Trail of Tears" refers to? Write it down now and compare it with what you know at the end.

Cold open · Cherokee Nation, spring 1838

Soldiers came to Rebecca Neugin's door when she was three years old.

"When the soldiers came to our house my father wanted to fight, but my mother told him that the soldiers would kill him if he did and we surrendered without a fight. They drove us out of our house to join other prisoners in a stockade."
Rebecca Neugin, recalling 1838, as recorded by historian Grant Foreman in 1932
The question: Her nation had a constitution, a newspaper, and a Supreme Court ruling on its side.
How did a nation that won in court end up in a stockade?

Source: Rebecca Neugin, in Grant Foreman, Indian Removal (University of Oklahoma Press; 1974 printing, p. 242).

We start with one family on one day. In the spring of 1838, U.S. soldiers arrived at the farm of a Cherokee family in the southern Appalachians. One of the children was a little girl named Rebecca, about three years old.

Read her words on the slide. Her father wanted to fight. Her mother stopped him, because she knew the soldiers would kill him. The family surrendered and was driven to a stockade, a log-walled pen where the army held prisoners. Her mother begged to go back for bedding and a few cooking pots. Everything else stayed behind.

How do we know this? Rebecca Neugin lived to be an old woman in Oklahoma, and in 1932 the historian Grant Foreman wrote down her memory. That makes it a memory recorded almost a century later, so we will test it against sources written in 1838.

The picture is an AI-generated interpretation, not evidence. It shows the moment she describes without showing violence.

Here is the puzzle for today. Her nation had done everything Americans said a "civilized" people should do. It even won its case in the Supreme Court. So how did it end here? You will see this family again at the very end.

Check yourself: Why does it matter that this account was recorded in 1932 rather than in 1838?

The homeland · 1820s

The Cherokee Nation held its homeland where four states met, and Georgia claimed it.

The land: farms, towns, and a capital at New Echota, in today's northwest Georgia.
The people: about 16,000 Cherokee still lived in the East in 1835.
The neighbors: Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole; some 60,000 people in five nations.
The claim: Georgia said every acre inside its borders belonged under Georgia law.
The Cherokee were not a remnant. They were a nation with borders, and Georgia drew its own borders around them.

Five Tribes: the five southeastern nations removed in the 1830s. White Americans later called them the "Five Civilized Tribes," a label that ranked peoples by how much they resembled white Americans.

Sources: Perdue & Green, The Cherokee Nation and the Trail of Tears (2007); 1835 Cherokee census (Henderson Roll); course case study, "Jacksonian Indian Removal."

Before the removal, there was a homeland. In the 1820s the Cherokee Nation covered the mountains and valleys where Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama, and North Carolina meet. Its capital, New Echota, sat in what is now northwest Georgia.

Most Cherokee were farmers. They raised corn, hogs, and cattle, and some ran mills, ferries, and stores. A census in 1835 counted about 16,000 Cherokee in the East.

They had neighbors in the same situation: the Creek, also called the Muscogee; the Choctaw; the Chickasaw; and the Seminole in Florida. Together these five nations numbered roughly 60,000 people. Read the gloss at the bottom: white Americans later called them the "Five Civilized Tribes," a label that judged them by how much they looked like white society. We will just say the Five Tribes.

Look at the map. It is a real 1830 map of Georgia, and in the northwest corner it labels "Cherokee Indians." Even the mapmaker knew it was their land. But Georgia claimed it too.

Why this matters: this is a story about two governments claiming the same ground.

Check yourself: Name the five southeastern nations removed in the 1830s.

Building a nation · 1821–1828

The Cherokee built a written language, a constitution, and a newspaper.

1821: Sequoyah finished a syllabary; within a few years thousands of Cherokee could read and write.
1827: a written constitution created a legislature, courts, and a principal chief.
1828: the Cherokee Phoenix, edited by Elias Boudinot, printed in English and Cherokee.
A hard truth: by 1835 wealthy Cherokee planters held more than 1,500 enslaved Black people.
The Cherokee did what U.S. "civilization" policy asked. It made them a stronger nation, not a safer one.

Syllabary: a writing system in which each symbol stands for a syllable. Sequoyah's had 86 symbols.

For thirty years, U.S. officials had told Native nations to farm, go to school, and govern themselves like Americans. The Cherokee took that advice further than anyone expected.

First, writing. Around 1821 a Cherokee silversmith named Sequoyah finished a syllabary, a set of symbols for every syllable in the Cherokee language. It was so easy to learn that within a few years thousands of Cherokee were reading and writing letters in their own language.

Second, government. In 1827 the Cherokee wrote a constitution with a legislature, courts, and an elected principal chief. In 1828 they launched a newspaper, the Cherokee Phoenix, printed at New Echota in English and Cherokee. Its editor was Elias Boudinot; remember his name.

Look at the two images. Both are real: Sequoyah holding his syllabary, from an 1836 print, and the first page of the Phoenix.

There is a hard truth in the red box. Copying the plantation South also meant copying slavery. By 1835 Cherokee planters held more than 1,500 enslaved Black people.

Why this matters: a nation with a constitution looked more like a rival state, and Georgia treated it that way.

Check yourself: Why might a written constitution make Georgia more hostile, not less?

Georgia's claim · 1802–1832

Georgia wanted Cherokee land, and gold made it want it faster.

1802: the U.S. promised Georgia it would end Indian land titles in the state "as early as the same can be peaceably obtained, on reasonable terms."
1828–1829: gold near today's Dahlonega; thousands of prospectors poured into Cherokee country.
1828–1830: Georgia declared Cherokee laws void and barred Cherokee from testifying against whites.
1832: a state lottery handed Cherokee land to white Georgians.
Georgia did not wait for removal. It made staying unbearable.

Sources: Articles of Agreement and Cession (Compact of 1802); Georgia acts of 1828–1830; Perdue & Green (2007); Saunt, Unworthy Republic (2020).

Now the pressure. In 1802 Georgia gave up its claim to western lands, which became Alabama and Mississippi. In return, the federal government promised to end Indian land titles inside Georgia "as early as the same can be peaceably obtained, on reasonable terms." For twenty-five years Georgians reminded Washington of that promise.

Cotton raised the stakes. The upland South was turning into cotton country, and planters and small farmers wanted more ground. Then, in 1828 and 1829, gold was found in the Cherokee hills near today's Dahlonega, and thousands of prospectors rushed in.

Georgia's legislature acted between 1828 and 1830. It extended state law over the Cherokee Nation, declared Cherokee laws void, and barred Cherokee from testifying against white people in Georgia courts. A Cherokee whose farm was robbed had no way to win in court. In 1832 Georgia held a lottery that gave Cherokee land to white citizens.

The image is an AI-generated interpretation of the gold rush: crowded creek below, a Cherokee family watching above.

Check yourself: List two Georgia laws that made life harder for Cherokee who stayed.

The president · 1814–1830

Andrew Jackson came to the White House determined to move the southern nations west.

1814: after defeating the Red Stick Creeks, General Jackson imposed the Treaty of Fort Jackson, taking about 23 million acres, including land of Creeks who had fought beside him.
1829: President Jackson told the Cherokee and Creek he would not stop states from ruling over them.
His argument: move west, beyond the states, and survive; stay, and live under state law.
Jackson called removal a kindness. The people being moved called it exile.

Sources: Treaty of Fort Jackson (1814); Remini, Andrew Jackson and His Indian Wars (2001); Howe, What Hath God Wrought (2007).

Georgia had an ally in the White House. Andrew Jackson, elected in 1828, had built his fame fighting Native nations as well as the British.

In 1814, during the Creek War, Jackson's army crushed the Red Sticks, a militant Creek faction, at Horseshoe Bend. The peace he dictated, the Treaty of Fort Jackson, took about 23 million acres from the Creek Nation, including land belonging to Creeks who had fought on Jackson's side.

As president, Jackson took Georgia's side. In 1829 he told the Cherokee and Creek that the federal government would not protect them from state laws. Their choice, as he framed it, was to move west, beyond any state, or stay and live as subjects of Georgia or Alabama.

The portrait is real, painted by Ralph Earl in 1817, when Jackson was still a general.

Why this matters: Jackson sincerely believed removal was best for everyone, including Native people. He also believed white settlers had a better claim to the land. Both beliefs pushed the same way.

Check yourself: What choice did Jackson say the southern nations faced?

Primary source · Jackson's Second Annual Message, December 6, 1830

How did Jackson explain removal to Congress?

"It gives me pleasure to announce to Congress that the benevolent policy of the Government, steadily pursued for nearly thirty years, in relation to the removal of the Indians beyond the white settlements is approaching to a happy consummation. . . .

What good man would prefer a country covered with forests and ranged by a few thousand savages to our extensive Republic, studded with cities, towns, and prosperous farms . . . ?"
Andrew Jackson, Second Annual Message to Congress, December 6, 1830

Read closely, on your own:

  1. Which words does Jackson use to make removal sound generous?
  2. Whose view of the land does his question leave out?

Consummation: completion. Benevolent: kind, well-meaning.

Here is Jackson in his own words. Every December the president sent Congress an annual message, what we now call the State of the Union. In 1830 Jackson used his to celebrate removal.

Read the first sentence. He calls the policy "benevolent," meaning kind, and says it is nearing a "happy consummation," a happy completion. Elsewhere in the same message he promised that removal would free the tribes from the power of the states and let them live "in their own way."

Now read the second sentence, his question. He pictures Native land as empty forest "ranged by a few thousand savages" and asks what good man would not prefer farms and cities. Notice what that leaves out: Cherokee farms, mills, and towns already stood on that land.

The image is the real first page of the message, from the National Archives.

How to read it: this is the voice from the top. Next we will hear the voice of the people being removed.

Check yourself: What does the word "benevolent" ask Congress to believe about removal?

The law · May 28, 1830

Congress passed the Indian Removal Act by five votes.

The deal: the president could trade western land to tribes "as may choose to exchange" their eastern homes.
The promise: the U.S. would "forever secure and guaranty" the new land, with $500,000 to pay the costs.
The vote: Senate 28–19; House 102–97. Senator Theodore Frelinghuysen and Rep. Davy Crockett opposed it.
On paper, removal was a choice. Georgia's laws and Jackson's pressure took the choice away.

Sources: An Act to provide for an exchange of lands with the Indians residing in any of the states or territories, May 28, 1830 (4 Stat. 411); Register of Debates, 21st Congress, 1st Session.

In the spring of 1830 Congress debated removal for weeks, and it was close. The Senate passed the bill 28 to 19. The House passed it 102 to 97, a margin of five votes. Jackson signed it on May 28, 1830.

Read what the law actually said. It let the president trade land west of the Mississippi to tribes "as may choose to exchange" their eastern lands. It promised that the United States would "forever secure and guaranty" the new western lands to them. It set aside $500,000 to pay for it all.

Notice the word "choose." The act did not order anyone removed by force. But Georgia's laws were already making life impossible, and Jackson would not protect the tribes from those laws.

Opponents saw this. Senator Theodore Frelinghuysen of New Jersey spoke against the bill for about six hours over three days, and Congressman Davy Crockett of Tennessee voted no.

The image is a real page from the printed Senate debate.

Check yourself: Why is the phrase "as may choose to exchange" important for judging the act?

Primary source · Cherokee address to the people of the United States, July 1830

"We wish to remain on the land of our fathers."

"We are not willing to remove . . . We wish to remain on the land of our fathers. We have a perfect and original right to remain without interruption or molestation. The treaties with us, and laws of the United States made in pursuance of treaties, guaranty our residence and our privileges, and secure us against intruders."
Cherokee Nation, address to the people of the United States, July 1830; printed in the Cherokee Phoenix, July 24, 1830

Read closely, on your own:

  1. What two things do the Cherokee say protect their right to stay?
  2. How does this answer Jackson's picture of empty forest?

Memorial: a formal written petition to a government. Molestation: harassment, interference.

The Cherokee answered with the tools of a free press and a free people. In 1830 they sent memorials, formal petitions, to Congress, and that July the Cherokee government addressed the American people directly. The Cherokee Phoenix printed the address, and newspapers across the country reprinted it.

Read the slide. "We are not willing to remove." "We wish to remain on the land of our fathers." Then comes the legal argument: treaties with the United States, and federal laws made under those treaties, guarantee their right to stay. Treaties, under the Constitution, are part of the supreme law of the land.

Elsewhere the address says the western country "is not the land of our birth, nor of our affections." This is not a plea for pity. It is a nation arguing its rights.

The image shows signatures on a Cherokee memorial to Congress from February 1830, written in both English and Sequoyah's syllabary. You are looking at the syllabary from the last slide being used to defend the homeland.

Check yourself: Is this address an emotional appeal, a legal argument, or both? Give one phrase as evidence.

Appeal to the courts · 1831–1832

The Cherokee took Georgia to the Supreme Court, and in 1832 they won.

1831, Cherokee Nation v. Georgia: the Court called the Cherokee a "domestic dependent nation" and would not hear the suit.
1831: Georgia sentenced missionary Samuel Worcester to four years at hard labor for living in the Nation without a state license.
March 1832, Worcester v. Georgia: the Cherokee Nation is "a distinct community . . . in which the laws of Georgia can have no force."
The highest court in the land agreed with the Cherokee.

Sources: Cherokee Nation v. Georgia, 30 U.S. 1 (1831); Worcester v. Georgia, 31 U.S. 515 (1832).

Next the Cherokee went to court. In 1831 they sued Georgia in the Supreme Court. Chief Justice John Marshall, whom you met in Lecture 1, ruled that the Cherokee were not a foreign nation but a "domestic dependent nation," something like a ward under a guardian, so the Court would not hear the suit. It was a loss, but a narrow one.

Then Georgia gave them a better case. A Georgia law required every white person living in the Cherokee Nation to get a state license and swear loyalty to Georgia. A missionary from Vermont named Samuel Worcester refused. Georgia arrested him and sentenced him to four years at hard labor.

His appeal, Worcester v. Georgia, reached the Court in 1832, and Marshall ruled for him and for the Cherokee. Read the quotation: the Cherokee Nation was "a distinct community" in which "the laws of Georgia can have no force." Only the federal government could deal with the Cherokee, through treaties.

Why this matters: the Cherokee had now won on the highest legal ground the United States offered.

Check yourself: What did Worcester v. Georgia say about Georgia's laws inside the Cherokee Nation?

The answer · 1832–1833

Georgia ignored the ruling, and Jackson would not enforce it.

Georgia: refused to free Worcester; he stayed in prison until January 1833.
Jackson, April 7, 1832: the decision "has fell still born, and they find that it cannot coerce Georgia to yield to its mandate."
The famous line "John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it" first appeared in print in 1864. He probably never said it.
1832: Georgia's lottery gave away Cherokee land while Cherokee families still lived on it.
A court can say what the law is. It cannot make a president act.

Sources: Jackson to John Coffee, April 7, 1832, in Correspondence of Andrew Jackson, ed. Bassett, vol. 4; Horace Greeley, The American Conflict (1864); Perdue & Green (2007).

The Cherokee celebrated, but the victory went nowhere. Georgia simply ignored the Supreme Court and kept Samuel Worcester in prison.

Enforcing a court ruling is the president's job, and Jackson did nothing. Read his private letter from April 7, 1832: the decision had "fell still born," born dead, because the Court could not force Georgia to obey.

You may have heard the line "John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it." It first appeared in print in 1864, decades after Jackson's death, and historians doubt he said it. His real letter is just as revealing.

Worcester finally left prison in January 1833, after he stopped his legal fight and the governor pardoned him. Meanwhile Georgia ran its lottery. The image shows a real land grant from it: a piece of the Cherokee Nation given to a white Georgian, while Cherokee families still farmed it.

Why this matters: the Cherokee's best argument was legal, and the law turned out to be only as strong as the people willing to enforce it.

Check yourself: Why did winning in the Supreme Court not save the Cherokee homeland?

The other four nations · 1830–1842

The Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, and Seminole lost their homelands too, or fought.

Choctaw, 1831–1833: the first nation removed under the act; blizzards and cholera killed thousands.
Creek, 1836–1837: after fraud and violence, the army removed about 15,000 people, some in chains.
Chickasaw, 1837–1838: paid for their own removal from the sale of their land.
Seminole, 1835–1842: fought the Second Seminole War; several hundred stayed in Florida.

Each nation's story continues in the Pierian Spring: Choctaw · Creek · Chickasaw · Seminole

Sources: Foreman, Indian Removal (1932); Akers, Living in the Land of Death (2004); Saunt, Unworthy Republic (2020). Death tolls are estimates.

Before we follow the Cherokee to the end, look at the map. The Cherokee were not the first to go. While they fought in court, the other four nations were already losing their homelands.

The Choctaw of Mississippi signed the first removal treaty under the new act in 1830 and moved west between 1831 and 1833, through blizzards and then a cholera epidemic. Estimates of the dead run into the thousands.

The Creek of Alabama were cheated out of their land by speculators. When some fought back in 1836, the army removed about 15,000 Creek, some of the men in chains.

The Chickasaw negotiated harder and paid for their own removal out of the money from selling their land, but they still suffered disease and hunger on the way.

The Seminole of Florida fought. The Second Seminole War lasted from 1835 to 1842, and several hundred Seminole were never removed.

Each of these stories gets its own slide in the Pierian Spring section at the end.

Check yourself: Which nation was removed first under the Removal Act, and which fought a seven-year war?

A nation divided · 1832–1835

A small Cherokee faction decided that a bad treaty was better than none.

National Party: Principal Chief John Ross and most Cherokee refused to sell.
Treaty Party: Major Ridge, his son John Ridge, and his nephew Elias Boudinot believed removal could not be stopped.
1832: Boudinot resigned from the Phoenix when the council would not let him print the case for a treaty.
Cherokee law, 1829: selling national land without the nation's consent was punishable by death.
Both sides wanted the Cherokee to survive. They disagreed about whether staying was possible.
Names: Elias Boudinot was born Gallegina, or Buck, Watie; he took the name of a New Jersey patron. Major Ridge's Cherokee name was Kahnungdatlageh.

After 1832, the Cherokee faced a terrible question. Was there any way left to stay?

Most said yes, or at least that they would never sell. Their leader was the principal chief, John Ross, and his supporters were called the National Party.

A smaller group said no. Major Ridge, an elder and war hero; his son John Ridge; and his nephew Elias Boudinot, the newspaper editor, came to believe removal could not be stopped. Better, they argued, to sign a treaty now and get money and western land than to lose everything for nothing. They became known as the Treaty Party.

In 1832 Boudinot resigned as editor of the Phoenix after the council would not let him print that argument.

Read the red box. In 1829 the Cherokee had written into law that selling national land without the nation's consent was punishable by death. Major Ridge himself had supported that principle. Keep it in mind.

The names box helps with the two names you may meet in your sources.

Check yourself: What did the Treaty Party believe that the National Party did not?

The treaty · New Echota, December 29, 1835

At New Echota, a few hundred Cherokee agreed to sell the whole homeland.

Who: a few hundred Cherokee at most, out of about 16,000; roughly twenty men signed.
The terms: all land east of the Mississippi for $5 million and land in Indian Territory; two years to move.
Not authorized: the Cherokee National Council never approved it; Ross was in Washington.
May 1836: the Senate ratified it 31–15, exactly the two-thirds required; one vote fewer and it would have failed.
The treaty was law to the United States and a fraud to the Cherokee Nation.

Sources: Treaty with the Cherokee, December 29, 1835 (7 Stat. 478); Perdue & Green (2007); Smithsonian NMAI, Nation to Nation.

In December 1835 a U.S. commissioner, the Reverend John Schermerhorn, called a meeting at the Cherokee capital, New Echota. He warned that anyone who stayed away would be counted as agreeing. Most Cherokee stayed away anyway.

A few hundred people came, out of about 16,000. On December 29, roughly twenty Treaty Party men signed the Treaty of New Echota. The Cherokee would give up every acre east of the Mississippi in exchange for five million dollars and land in Indian Territory, today's Oklahoma, and they would have two years to leave.

Principal Chief John Ross was in Washington at the time with the nation's official delegation. The Cherokee National Council never approved the treaty.

The U.S. Senate ratified it anyway in May 1836, by 31 to 15. Treaties need two-thirds of the senators voting. Thirty-one was exactly enough; one vote fewer and the treaty would have failed.

The image is an AI-generated interpretation of the signing, not a record of the room.

Why this matters: from now on, the United States could say it was only enforcing a treaty.

Check yourself: Give two reasons most Cherokee considered the Treaty of New Echota illegitimate.

Primary source · John Ross to the U.S. Senate and House, September 28, 1836

"We are denationalized; we are disfranchised."

"By the stipulations of this instrument, we are despoiled of our private possessions . . . Our property may be plundered before our eyes; violence may be committed on our persons; even our lives may be taken away, and there is none to regard our complaints. We are denationalized; we are disfranchised. We are deprived of membership in the human family!"
John Ross, letter from Red Clay Council Ground, Cherokee Nation, September 28, 1836
1838: Ross carried to Congress a protest signed by 15,665 Cherokee. Congress did not act.

Read closely, on your own:

  1. What does Ross say the treaty takes besides land?
  2. Why might he call it an "instrument" rather than a treaty?

Despoiled: robbed. Denationalized: stripped of their nation. Disfranchised: stripped of political rights.

This is John Ross, principal chief of the Cherokee Nation. His father was Scottish and his mother part Cherokee, and he grew up speaking English more easily than Cherokee. But the Cherokee people trusted him, and they re-elected him for decades.

In September 1836, Ross wrote to Congress about the Treaty of New Echota. Read the slide. He refuses even to call it a treaty; he calls it "this instrument." Then he lists what it takes: property, legal protection, safety, their nation, their political rights, and finally their "membership in the human family."

Ross did not only write. In 1838 he brought Congress a protest signed by 15,665 Cherokee, nearly the whole nation. Congress took no action.

The portrait is a real lithograph from the 1840s.

How to read it: Ross is a political leader making a case to lawmakers. His language is dramatic on purpose. Ask whether the events that followed bore his warnings out.

Check yourself: Why does Ross put "membership in the human family" last in his list?

Check yourself · on your own

Can you explain how the Cherokee fought removal without going to war?

Answer from memory, in a sentence or two each:

  1. Name three peaceful tools the Cherokee used to defend their homeland between 1827 and 1838.
  2. Why didn't the Supreme Court's 1832 ruling protect them?
  3. Why did the Treaty Party sign at New Echota, and why did most Cherokee reject the treaty?

When you have written your answers, compare them with these possible answers.

×

Possible answers

  1. Any three: a written constitution (1827); the bilingual Cherokee Phoenix (1828); memorials and an address to Congress and the public (1830); lawsuits in the Supreme Court (1831, 1832); Ross's protests and the 15,665-name petition (1836–1838).
  2. The Court had no power to enforce its ruling. Georgia ignored it, and President Jackson, who supported removal, refused to make Georgia comply.
  3. The Treaty Party believed removal could not be stopped and hoped to get money and land before losing everything. Most Cherokee rejected the treaty because a small, unauthorized group signed it without the National Council's approval.

Pause here and test yourself before the story turns violent. Trying to recall something and then checking helps you remember it far better than rereading does.

The deadline · May 1838

When the deadline passed, General Winfield Scott told the Cherokee that the army had come.

"Cherokees! The President of the United States has sent me with a powerful army . . . The full moon of May is already on the wane; and before another shall have passed away, every Cherokee man, woman and child . . . must be in motion to join their brethren in the far West."
General Winfield Scott, address to the Cherokee, May 10, 1838
The president: Martin Van Buren, Jackson's successor, kept the policy.
By May 23, 1838: only about 2,000 Cherokee had gone west. Scott had about 7,000 regulars and militia.
Scott called his soldiers "your friends." He also called resistance and escape "hopeless."

Sources: Winfield Scott, Address to the Cherokee Nation, May 10, 1838; NPS, "The Trail of Tears and the Forced Relocation of the Cherokee Nation."

The treaty gave the Cherokee two years, until May 23, 1838. Jackson left office in 1837, and his successor, Martin Van Buren, kept the policy.

When the deadline came, only about 2,000 Cherokee had moved west, most of them Treaty Party families. Roughly 16,000 were still at home, many still hoping Ross could stop it.

Van Buren sent General Winfield Scott with about 7,000 soldiers, a mix of regular army and state militia. On May 10, 1838, Scott issued the address on the slide. Read it: "every Cherokee man, woman and child" must be moving west before the next full moon.

The rest of the address mixes a threat with a plea. Scott calls the troops "your friends," but says there are enough of them to make resistance and escape "hopeless." He calls himself "an old warrior" and begs the Cherokee to spare him "the horror of witnessing the destruction of the Cherokees."

The photograph of Scott is real, taken about a decade later.

Check yourself: Who is included in Scott's phrase "every Cherokee man, woman and child," and who is left out?

The roundup · May–June 1838

Soldiers went from farm to farm, and families had minutes to leave.

May 26, 1838: the roundup began in Georgia, then spread to Tennessee, Alabama, and North Carolina.
Seized: people were taken in fields, on roads, and at home, often with only the clothes they wore.
Behind the troops: settlers took livestock, furniture, and houses.
"The Cherokees are nearly all prisoners. They have been dragged from their houses, and encamped at the forts and military posts, all over the nation."
Evan Jones, Baptist missionary, Camp Hetzel, Tennessee, June 16, 1838

Sources: Evan Jones, letter of June 16, 1838 (Baptist Missionary Magazine, 1838); Perdue & Green (2007); Neugin in Foreman (1932).

On May 26, 1838, the roundup began in Georgia, where state militia did much of the work, and over the next weeks it spread to Tennessee, Alabama, and North Carolina.

Soldiers went from farm to farm. People were taken while plowing, walking on the road, or eating dinner. Many left with only the clothes they wore. Remember Rebecca Neugin's mother begging to go back for bedding: that was this moment.

Behind the soldiers came settlers. They drove off cattle and hogs, carried off furniture, and moved into houses still warm from the families who had lived there.

Read the quotation. Evan Jones was a white Baptist missionary who had lived among the Cherokee for years. On June 16, 1838, he wrote from a camp in Tennessee: "The Cherokees are nearly all prisoners." Notice his word: prisoners, not emigrants.

The painting is an AI-generated interpretation: families on the road, settlers waiting by an empty farm.

Why this matters: what the law called an exchange of lands now looked like the arrest of a whole people.

Check yourself: Why does Jones choose the word "prisoners"?

The stockades · summer 1838

Thousands waited in stockades and camps through a summer of heat and disease.

The camps: forts and holding camps, the largest near the Cherokee Agency on the Hiwassee River in Tennessee.
June 1838: the army sent about 2,800 people west by river; heat and sickness were so deadly that Scott halted removal until fall.
Disease: dysentery, measles, and whooping cough spread through crowded camps.
Ross's request: the Cherokee won the right to run their own removal, in 13 detachments, once the heat broke.
The dying started before the walking.

Sources: NPS, Trail of Tears National Historic Trail; Perdue & Green (2007); Thornton, "Cherokee Population Losses" (1984).

The prisoners were marched to stockades, log-walled forts, and then to larger holding camps, many near the Cherokee Agency on the Hiwassee River in southeastern Tennessee.

In June the army tried to send the first groups west by river, about 2,800 people in three detachments. It was a drought summer, rivers ran low, and the heat and sickness were so deadly that Scott stopped further removal until the weather cooled.

That meant months of waiting in crowded camps with poor water and poor food. Dysentery, measles, and whooping cough spread fast, and children and elders died first. Hundreds died before the main journey began; some estimates run higher.

John Ross then won a concession: the Cherokee themselves would organize the rest of the removal, in thirteen detachments with Cherokee leaders, paid for out of treaty funds.

The image is an AI-generated interpretation of a camp, not a picture of a real one.

Why this matters: the deaths were not only on the trail. Holding people in crowded camps for months was itself deadly.

Check yourself: Why did Scott delay the main removal until fall?

The trail · October 1838–March 1839

Most Cherokee traveled about 1,000 miles west through a bitter winter.

Detachments: groups of about 1,000, led by Cherokee conductors, left between August and December 1838.
The road: most went overland through Tennessee, Kentucky, Illinois, Missouri, and Arkansas, on foot, with the sick in wagons.
Winter: ice on the Ohio and Mississippi stranded groups for weeks in southern Illinois.
February 1839: Ross's wife, Quatie, died near Little Rock.
Every delay meant more days of cold, short rations, and graves beside the road.

Sources: NPS, Trail of Tears National Historic Trail; Foreman, Indian Removal (1932); Perdue & Green (2007).

In late summer and fall of 1838 the Cherokee-led detachments set out, each of about a thousand people with wagons, horses, and oxen.

Most took a northern overland route: across Tennessee and Kentucky, over the Ohio River into southern Illinois, across the Mississippi into Missouri, and down through Arkansas into Indian Territory. Depending on the route, the journey ran roughly 800 to 1,200 miles. Most people walked. The sick, the old, and the youngest rode in wagons.

The winter of 1838 to 1839 was hard. Ice on the Ohio and Mississippi stopped several detachments for weeks in southern Illinois, camped in the snow, with too little food and too few blankets. People died of pneumonia, exposure, and disease, and were buried beside the road.

John Ross's wife, Quatie, died near Little Rock in February 1839. The last detachments arrived in March.

The image is an AI-generated interpretation of a winter camp by the Mississippi.

Check yourself: Name two natural obstacles that slowed the detachments, and explain why delay was deadly.

The cost · 1838–1839

About 4,000 Cherokee died in the roundup, the camps, and on the trail, and possibly many more.

~16,000
Cherokee forced west, 1838–1839
~4,000
deaths: the most-cited estimate
2,000–8,000
range of scholarly estimates
The 4,000 figure: estimated by Dr. Elizur Butler, a missionary doctor who traveled with a detachment.
Higher: demographer Russell Thornton (1984) argued the toll may have been about twice that.
Why a range: records were incomplete, and studies count different months and kinds of loss.
However historians count, roughly one Cherokee in four or five died.

Sources: Thornton, "Cherokee Population Losses during the Trail of Tears: A New Perspective and a New Estimate," Ethnohistory 31:4 (1984); Foreman (1932); Perdue & Green (2007).

How many died? Historians give a range, and you should learn both the common number and the reasons for the range.

About 16,000 Cherokee were forced west. The figure you will see most often is about 4,000 deaths in the roundup, the camps, and on the trail. It goes back to Dr. Elizur Butler, a missionary physician who traveled with one detachment and made an estimate in 1839.

Some studies have come in lower, near 2,000. In 1984 the demographer Russell Thornton argued the true loss may have been about twice the usual figure, around 8,000, once you count everyone who died from removal's effects over the whole period, including the first year in the West.

Why so much uncertainty? Detachment records are incomplete, and studies count different things over different months.

So use careful language: "about 4,000 is the most-cited estimate, and some historians argue it was higher." Either way, roughly one in four or five died.

Check yourself: Explain in one sentence why the Cherokee death toll is given as a range.

Arrival · Indian Territory, 1839

The survivors rebuilt a nation in the West, but removal's wounds turned deadly.

Rebuilding: new farms, schools, and a capital at Tahlequah, in today's Oklahoma.
June 22, 1839: Major Ridge, John Ridge, and Elias Boudinot were killed by Cherokee who held them guilty under the law against selling land.
July 1839: an Act of Union joined eastern and western Cherokee under one constitution.
Those who stayed: several hundred Cherokee in the North Carolina mountains became the ancestors of today's Eastern Band.
Removal emptied a homeland. It did not end a nation.

Sources: Perdue & Green (2007); Cherokee Nation, Act of Union (1839); Pierian Spring: the Treaty Party · those who stayed.

The survivors arrived in Indian Territory, in what is now eastern Oklahoma, sick, grieving, and short of everything. They began again: clearing fields, building cabins, opening schools, and setting up a new capital at Tahlequah.

But the old divisions came west with them. On June 22, 1839, groups of Cherokee killed Major Ridge, John Ridge, and Elias Boudinot on the same day. The killers saw it as carrying out the 1829 law against selling national land. John Ross said he had not known of the plan. Violence between the factions went on for years.

In July 1839 an Act of Union joined the newly arrived Cherokee with those who had moved west earlier under one constitution.

Not everyone left. Several hundred Cherokee in the North Carolina mountains managed to stay, and their descendants form today's Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians.

The image is an AI-generated interpretation of rebuilding.

Why this matters: the Cherokee Nation survived, and still exists today, but removal reshaped it.

Check yourself: Why were Major Ridge, John Ridge, and Elias Boudinot killed in 1839?

Check yourself · on your own

Can you explain how removal was carried out, from deadline to arrival?

Answer from memory, in a sentence or two each:

  1. What happened to Cherokee families after the May 23, 1838 deadline passed?
  2. Why did many people die before the march west even began?
  3. Why do historians give the Cherokee death toll as a range rather than a single number?

When you have written your answers, compare them with these possible answers.

×

Possible answers

  1. General Scott's soldiers and state militia rounded them up from their homes and fields, often with only what they could carry, and held them in stockades and camps; settlers took their property.
  2. Thousands were crowded into camps for months in a hot, dry summer with poor water and food, so diseases like dysentery, measles, and whooping cough spread. The first river detachments in June also suffered heavy losses.
  3. Records were incomplete, and studies count different things: deaths on the trail only, or also in the camps and the first year in the West, or the total population loss. About 4,000 is the most-cited estimate; some argue for about 8,000.

Second pause. Write your answers before you open the popup.

Tips for question 2: the stockades slide has the answer. Think about weather, crowding, water, and how long people waited.

After this, the lecture changes direction. You now know what happened. Next you will learn a word historians use to describe events like this, and the tool your capstone uses to test whether it fits.

Naming it · from the 1830s to the 1990s

Historians now ask whether a newer word fits this older story: ethnic cleansing.

Where the term came from

It spread in 1991–1992 from Serbian and Croatian etničko čišćenje, used by perpetrators and nationalist media in the wars of Yugoslavia's breakup. Western journalists and diplomats adopted it.

Why it is uncomfortable

"Cleansing" was a euphemism. It made driving people out sound like cleaning something dirty. When we use the term, we should remember whose word it was.

What it is not

It is not a crime defined on its own in international law, as genocide is. It is a descriptive term; the acts it describes can be prosecuted as crimes against humanity.

The word is new. The question is old: when is moving a people really driving them out?

Euphemism: a mild word used in place of a harsh one. Anachronism: judging the past with ideas from a later time; this is why you will test the term against evidence instead of assuming it.

Source: course framework, "Understanding Ethnic Cleansing".

You now know what happened. The lecture turns from telling the story to analyzing it, and the first thing you need is a word.

The term "ethnic cleansing" entered English in 1991 and 1992, during the wars that broke Yugoslavia apart. It came from the Serbian and Croatian phrase etničko čišćenje, used by the perpetrators and nationalist media themselves. Western reporters and diplomats picked it up, and it became the standard term.

Notice the problem in the red card. "Cleansing" is a euphemism, a soft word for a harsh act. It makes driving people from their homes sound like cleaning something dirty. Your course framework asks you to remember that we are borrowing the perpetrators' language.

Notice also the gold card. Unlike genocide, ethnic cleansing is not defined as a separate crime in international law. It is a descriptive term, though the acts involved, such as forced deportation and persecution, can be prosecuted as crimes against humanity.

No one in the 1830s used this word. Applying it is a historian's judgment, made with evidence, not a label we stamp on automatically. That caution is part of good historical thinking.

Check yourself: Why does your course framework call the origin of the term "problematic"?

The capstone's definition

Your capstone defines ethnic cleansing as forced removal meant to make a territory homogeneous.

Working Definition: Ethnic Cleansing"Ethnic cleansing is the systematic forced removal of an ethnic, racial, or religious group from a geographic area through violence, intimidation, forced deportation, or other coercive means, with the intent to create an ethnically homogeneous region. It is distinct from genocide in that the primary goal is removal rather than complete physical destruction (though the two can overlap)."

Systematic

Organized and deliberate, not random violence

Forced Removal

Displacement through coercion, not voluntary migration

Group Targeting

Based on ethnic, religious, or national identity

Territorial Goal

Creating homogeneous space

State/Militia Power

Requires organized force to implement

Sources: Trail of Tears worksheet, "Working Definition"; Key Elements from "Ethnic Cleansing: The Concept".

This is the definition your capstone worksheet uses, word for word. Read it slowly, because every phrase matters.

"Systematic": organized, not random. "Forced removal": people are made to leave, not choosing to. "An ethnic, racial, or religious group": people are targeted for who they are, not for anything they did. "Violence, intimidation, forced deportation, or other coercive means": force can be direct or can be pressure that leaves no real choice. "With the intent to create an ethnically homogeneous region": the goal is a territory that belongs to one group.

The last sentence draws a line. Ethnic cleansing aims to remove a people; genocide aims to destroy a people. The definition admits the two can overlap, and the Pierian Spring section shows historians arguing about exactly that for the 1830s.

The five cards come from the capstone's concept page. They are the same idea in short form: Systematic, Forced Removal, Group Targeting, Territorial Goal, and State or Militia Power.

Check yourself: In the definition, what separates ethnic cleansing from genocide?

The capstone's tool · Analytical Checklist

The worksheet tests a case against seven characteristics, one piece of evidence at a time.

1

Targeted Group Identification

Was a specific ethnic, racial, or religious group targeted?

2

Intent and Goal

Is there evidence of intent to remove the group from a territory?

3

Methods of Removal

Was forced deportation or relocation used?

4

Systematic Nature

Was the process organized or coordinated rather than random?

5

Scale and Scope

Were large numbers of people affected?

6

Accompanying Atrocities

Did mass killings or massacres occur?

7

Outcomes

Did the population demographics change significantly?

For each one

Mark Yes or No, cite evidence from the reader, then write a 2–4 sentence conclusion.

Source: Trail of Tears worksheet, "Analytical Checklist." Each characteristic has several more guiding questions on the worksheet; the first is shown here.

The worksheet turns the definition into a checklist of seven characteristics. On the slide you see each characteristic's name exactly as the worksheet prints it, with its first guiding question. The worksheet adds several more questions under each.

One: Targeted Group Identification. Was a specific group targeted? Two: Intent and Goal. Is there evidence of intent to remove the group? Three: Methods of Removal. Was forced deportation used? Four: Systematic Nature. Was it organized? Five: Scale and Scope. Were large numbers affected? Six: Accompanying Atrocities. Did mass killings occur? The worksheet also asks about cruel treatment and about property seized. Seven: Outcomes. Did the population change?

For each one, you decide yes or no and back it with evidence from the primary source reader. Then you write a short conclusion.

Two cards are in gold, Intent and Accompanying Atrocities. Those are the hardest to judge for Indian Removal, and two slides from now we will see why.

Check yourself: Without looking, name four of the seven characteristics.

Applying the tool · evidence from today's story

Today's story already gives you evidence for every characteristic.

CharacteristicEvidence you heard today (test it against the reader)
Targeted GroupThe act and treaty applied to Cherokee as a people, whatever an individual had done; Georgia barred Cherokee testimony against whites.
Intent and GoalJackson: removal "beyond the white settlements"; the act said tribes "may choose"; Georgia made staying unbearable.
Methods of RemovalScott's army and militia; roundup from homes; stockades and camps (Neugin, Evan Jones).
Systematic NatureA federal law, a treaty, a deadline, about 7,000 troops, planned detachments.
Scale and ScopeAbout 16,000 Cherokee; five nations and some 60,000 people across the Southeast.

Your verdict is yours to make in the worksheet. This table gives starting evidence, not answers.

Here is a head start. For each of the seven characteristics, the table points to evidence from today's lecture.

Targeted Group: the law and the treaty applied to the Cherokee as a people. It did not matter whether a family was rich or poor, Christian or traditional, for the treaty or against it. Georgia even barred Cherokee testimony against whites.

Intent and Goal: Jackson said he wanted the Indians "beyond the white settlements." But the act itself used the language of choice. That tension is something you must weigh.

Methods, Systematic Nature, and Scale are well documented: an army, a deadline, stockades, and about 16,000 people in this one nation alone.

Accompanying Atrocities and Outcomes: thousands died, property was seized, and the homeland changed hands.

Notice what the table does not do. It does not give you a verdict. Your job in the capstone is to test this evidence against the primary sources and decide for yourself.

Check yourself: Which characteristic do you think has the strongest evidence, and which the weakest?

Applying the tool · the hard cases

Two characteristics, intent and atrocities, demand the most careful judgment.

Intent and Goal

Removal, in his own words: Jackson wanted Native nations "beyond the white settlements."

But the language was choice: the act said "may choose"; Jackson called removal "benevolent."

Worksheet: "Were stated justifications (e.g., security, progress, civilization) used to legitimize removal?"

Accompanying Atrocities

No single great massacre marked the Cherokee removal of 1838.

But thousands died of disease, exposure, and hunger in conditions officials created and could foresee.

Worksheet: "Were basic needs (food, water, shelter, medical care) denied or withheld?"

Does a kind-sounding motive change the act? Does death by neglect count like death by violence? You will decide, with evidence.

Two characteristics take the most thought, and good answers will wrestle with them rather than skip past.

First, Intent and Goal. Jackson said plainly that he wanted Native nations "beyond the white settlements." That is a goal of removal from a territory. But he called the policy "benevolent," and the act spoke of tribes that "may choose" to exchange land. Does a kind-sounding justification change what the policy was? The worksheet asks exactly this: were justifications like progress or civilization used to make removal look legitimate?

Second, Accompanying Atrocities. In 1838 there was no single great massacre of Cherokee. Most of the deaths came from disease, exposure, and hunger in camps and on the road. Officials created those conditions and could see the deaths mounting. The worksheet asks whether basic needs were denied or withheld. Does death by neglect count as an atrocity?

Historians disagree about these questions, and the Pierian Spring section shows you two of them. Your conclusion should take a position and admit the strongest evidence against it.

Check yourself: Write one sentence of evidence for each side of the Intent question.

Bookend · Oklahoma, 1932

Nearly a century later, Rebecca Neugin still remembered the stockade.

1838: a three-year-old girl watched her mother stop her father from fighting.
In between: a constitution, a newspaper, petitions, a Supreme Court victory, a disputed treaty, an army, and a winter road.
1932: she told her story to a historian, and it became evidence.
The Cherokee answered with every peaceful tool a republic honors. The answer they got was the army.

Source: Rebecca Neugin, in Foreman, Indian Removal (1932).

We end where we began, with Rebecca Neugin. In 1838 she was three years old, watching her mother stop her father from fighting soldiers who would have killed him.

Think about everything that stood between her family and that morning. Her nation wrote a constitution and printed a newspaper in its own alphabet. It petitioned Congress and addressed the American people. It won in the Supreme Court. A small faction signed a treaty the nation never approved. Then the army came, and then the winter road.

In 1932, as an old woman in Oklahoma, she told the story to a historian. Her memory became evidence, the kind of evidence you will weigh in your capstone. The Cherokee Nation she belonged to still exists today, with its capital at Tahlequah.

Return to the sentence from the start: the Cherokee answered removal with every peaceful tool a republic honors, and the United States removed them anyway, by law and then by force.

The Pierian Spring was a spring sacred to the Muses in Greek myth. Alexander Pope's line means that a shallow taste of knowledge can mislead you; drink deeply.

This section is required. It tells the stories of the four other nations removed in the 1830s, what became of the Treaty Party, and the Cherokee who stayed in the East. It also shows how historians count the dead, how they argue over the words "ethnic cleansing" and "genocide," and how to handle doubtful sources. All of these will help you in the capstone.

Pierian Spring · The Creek (Muscogee), 1825–1837

The Creek lost their land to a forbidden treaty, then to fraud, and then to the army.

February 1825: William McIntosh signed the Treaty of Indian Springs, selling Creek land in Georgia against Creek law. On April 30, Creek warriors killed him under that law.
1826–1832: a new treaty replaced Indian Springs, but Georgia took the land anyway; in Alabama the 1832 Treaty of Cusseta gave Creek individual plots, and speculators cheated many out of them.
1836–1837: after some Creek fought back, the army removed about 15,000 people, some of the men in chains. In October 1837 the steamboat Monmouth sank on the Mississippi; about 300 Creek drowned.
Review question: How did both Creek law and U.S. treaties shape what happened to William McIntosh and to Creek land?

Sources: Green, The Politics of Indian Removal: Creek Government and Society in Crisis (1982); Saunt, Unworthy Republic (2020); Foreman (1932).

The Creek, who call themselves Muscogee, lived in Georgia and Alabama. Like the Cherokee, they had a national law forbidding any leader to sell land without the council's consent.

In February 1825 William McIntosh, a Creek leader allied with Georgia, signed the Treaty of Indian Springs anyway and sold Creek land in Georgia. On April 30, 1825, Creek warriors carried out the law: they surrounded his house and killed him. The federal government admitted the treaty was tainted and replaced it in 1826, but Georgia took the land anyway.

The Creek of Alabama then signed the Treaty of Cusseta in 1832. Instead of a nation's land, families got individual plots they could sell. Speculators cheated thousands of Creek out of them, sometimes by having the wrong person "sign" for a plot.

Starving and dispossessed, some Creek fought back in 1836. The army called it the Creek War and removed about 15,000 people, some of the men in chains. In October 1837 an overcrowded steamboat carrying Creek emigrants, the Monmouth, collided with another vessel on the Mississippi; about 300 died.

Check yourself: Answer the review question on the slide in three or four sentences.

Pierian Spring · The Choctaw, 1830–1833

The Choctaw were the first nation removed under the act, and they moved in the dead of winter.

September 1830: under heavy pressure, Choctaw leaders signed the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, giving up their Mississippi homeland.
1831–1833: removal in three waves met blizzards, floods, and cholera; estimates of the dead run to about 2,500, and some higher.
Article 14: families could stay as U.S. citizens on their own land, but officials and speculators blocked most claims.
"We as Choctaws rather chose to suffer and be free, than live under the degrading influence of laws, which our voice could not be heard in their formation."
George W. Harkins, farewell letter to the American people, 1832
Review question: What does Harkins mean by laws "which our voice could not be heard in their formation"?

Sources: Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek (1830); Akers, Living in the Land of Death (2004); Harkins, "Farewell Letter to the American People" (1832).

The Choctaw lived in central and southern Mississippi. In September 1830, months after the Removal Act passed, federal commissioners pressed Choctaw leaders into the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, the first removal treaty under the new law.

The Choctaw moved in three waves between 1831 and 1833. The first ran into one of the worst winters anyone remembered, the second into a cholera epidemic. Estimates of the dead are usually put around 2,500, and some historians give higher figures. The French writer Alexis de Tocqueville watched a group of Choctaw cross the Mississippi at Memphis in the winter of 1831 and wrote about it in Democracy in America.

Article 14 of the treaty let Choctaw families stay in Mississippi as U.S. citizens on their own land. In practice the federal agent failed to register many of the claims and speculators stripped others. Some Choctaw stayed anyway; their descendants form today's Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians.

Read George Harkins's words. He was a young Choctaw leader writing to the American people in 1832. His complaint is a democratic one: laws made without the consent of the governed.

Check yourself: Answer the review question on the slide in two or three sentences.

Pierian Spring · The Chickasaw, 1832–1838

The Chickasaw paid for their own removal, and it still cost them dearly.

October 1832: the Treaty of Pontotoc Creek ceded Chickasaw land in northern Mississippi; the land would be sold and the money used to pay for removal.
January 1837: with no western land of their own yet, the Chickasaw agreed at Doaksville to settle within the Choctaw Nation.
1837–1838: roughly 4,000–5,000 Chickasaw moved west with property and enslaved people; smallpox and spoiled government rations killed many in the West.
The lesson: even the best-negotiated removal was still removal.
Review question: Did negotiating better terms make Chickasaw removal any less forced? Use the definition's phrase "other coercive means" in your answer.

Sources: Treaty of Pontotoc Creek (1832); Treaty of Doaksville (1837); Paige, Bumpers & Littlefield, Chickasaw Removal (2010); Foreman (1932).

The Chickasaw lived in northern Mississippi and had watched what happened to their neighbors. They bargained hard.

In the Treaty of Pontotoc Creek, signed in October 1832, the Chickasaw gave up their land but insisted that it be sold and the money used to pay for their removal and support. They also refused to move until they found suitable land in the West.

In January 1837, at Doaksville, they agreed to settle inside the Choctaw Nation in Indian Territory. Between 1837 and 1838 roughly four to five thousand Chickasaw moved west, many with livestock and with the Black people they held in slavery.

Better terms did not mean safety. Smallpox broke out, and contractors supplied spoiled rations. Many died in their first year in the West.

Why this matters for your capstone: a negotiated removal can still be a coerced one, and the definition includes "other coercive means."

Check yourself: Answer the review question on the slide in three or four sentences.

Pierian Spring · The Seminole, 1832–1842

The Seminole fought removal for seven years, and some were never removed.

1832: some Seminole leaders signed the Treaty of Payne's Landing; many Seminole rejected it.
1835–1842: the Second Seminole War, the costliest U.S. war against a Native nation in this era.
October 1837: the army seized Osceola under a flag of truce; he died in prison in January 1838.
Black Seminoles: people of African descent, many escaped from slavery, lived and fought with the Seminole.
Review question: Why did the presence of Black Seminoles make white southerners more determined to remove the Seminole?

Sources: Mahon, History of the Second Seminole War (rev. 1985); Miller, Coacoochee's Bones (2003). Several hundred Seminole stayed in Florida.

The Seminole of Florida were a mix of Creek migrants and older Florida peoples. Living among them were Black Seminoles, people of African descent, many of them escaped from slavery in Georgia and the Carolinas.

In 1832 some Seminole leaders signed the Treaty of Payne's Landing. Many Seminole rejected it, and in December 1835 they went to war. The Second Seminole War lasted until 1842, cost the United States tens of millions of dollars and the lives of well over a thousand soldiers, and was the costliest of the removal-era wars.

Osceola became its best-known leader. In October 1837 General Thomas Jesup's troops seized him while he was meeting under a white flag of truce, an act many Americans at the time called dishonorable. He died in prison at Fort Moultrie, South Carolina, in January 1838.

Abraham, shown on the right, was a Black Seminole leader and interpreter who negotiated with U.S. officers.

In the end about 3,000 or more Seminole were removed west. Several hundred stayed hidden in the Everglades, and their descendants remain in Florida today.

Check yourself: Answer the review question on the slide in two or three sentences.

Pierian Spring · The Treaty Party, 1835–1846

The Treaty Party said it signed to save the Cherokee, and three of its leaders died for it.

Their argument: Georgia's pressure would destroy the Cherokee if they stayed; a treaty could at least secure money and land in the West.
1837: Boudinot answered Ross in print, accusing him of leading the people into false hope.
June 22, 1839: Major Ridge, John Ridge, and Boudinot were killed in separate attacks on the same day.
Survivor: Boudinot's brother Stand Watie escaped; feuding lasted until a treaty in 1846.
Review question: Were the Treaty Party realists or traitors? Make the strongest case for each side before giving your view.

Sources: Boudinot, Letters and Other Papers Relating to Cherokee Affairs (1837); Wilkins, Cherokee Tragedy: The Ridge Family and the Decimation of a People (rev. 1986).

The men of the Treaty Party were not simply sellouts, and they were not simply heroes either. Historians still argue about them.

Their argument was that Georgia's laws, the gold rush, and Jackson's refusal to help meant staying would end in ruin. A treaty, they said, would at least give the Cherokee money and land in the West. In 1837 Elias Boudinot published a long reply to John Ross, accusing him of keeping the people in false hope while their situation worsened.

But the treaty broke the nation's own law against selling land without consent, and most Cherokee never forgave them. On June 22, 1839, after removal, groups of Cherokee killed Major Ridge, John Ridge, and Elias Boudinot in separate attacks on the same day.

Boudinot's brother, Stand Watie, escaped. Violence between the factions went on for years, until a new treaty in 1846 brought an uneasy peace. Watie later became a Confederate general.

Check yourself: Answer the review question on the slide in a short paragraph.

Pierian Spring · Those who stayed, 1838–1868

Several hundred Cherokee stayed in the North Carolina mountains, and their descendants are still there.

The Oconaluftee Cherokee

Families along the Oconaluftee River lived on land outside the Nation's borders under an 1819 treaty, which gave them a legal claim to stay.

William Holland Thomas

A white trader adopted by the leader Yonaguska bought land for them in his own name, because North Carolina would not let them own it.

The Tsali story

In 1838 Tsali and his family killed two soldiers and Tsali was later executed. The legend that his sacrifice won the right to stay is not supported by the records.

Today the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians lives on the Qualla Boundary in western North Carolina.
Review question: Why might a community prefer the Tsali legend to the legal explanation of why it survived?

Sources: Finger, The Eastern Band of Cherokees, 1819–1900 (1984); Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900); Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians.

Not every Cherokee went west. In the mountains of western North Carolina, several hundred stayed, and their descendants form today's Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians.

Many of them were the Oconaluftee Cherokee. Under an 1819 treaty they had taken land just outside the Cherokee Nation's borders and accepted North Carolina citizenship, so the Treaty of New Echota did not clearly cover them. A white trader named William Holland Thomas, who had been adopted by the Cherokee leader Yonaguska, bought land for them in his own name, because state law would not let them hold title.

You may hear the story of Tsali. In late 1838 Tsali and members of his family killed two soldiers during the roundup. He was captured and executed. A later legend, popularized in the 1900s, says his sacrifice won the right of the others to stay. The records show the Oconaluftee had their own legal claim already, and historians treat the legend with caution.

The Eastern Band was recognized by the federal government after the Civil War and lives today on the Qualla Boundary.

Check yourself: Answer the review question on the slide in two or three sentences.

Pierian Spring · Counting the dead

Historians reach different death tolls because they count different things.

About 4,000

Dr. Elizur Butler, missionary doctor with a detachment, 1839. The most-cited figure.

About 4,000

James Mooney, ethnologist, 1900; he repeated the figure in his history of the Cherokee.

About 2,000

A 1973 study based on detachment records counted deaths during the journey itself.

About 8,000

Russell Thornton, 1984: deaths "may have been twice the generally accepted figure," counting population loss over the whole period.

The question behind every number: who is counted, where, and over how long?
Review question: Which estimate would you use in your capstone, and how would you describe the uncertainty in one honest sentence?

Sources: Thornton, Ethnohistory 31:4 (1984); Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900); Perdue & Green (2007).

Numbers feel solid, but each one comes from a method. Here are the main estimates of Cherokee deaths.

About 4,000 comes from Dr. Elizur Butler, a missionary physician who traveled west with a detachment and made his estimate in 1839, and the ethnologist James Mooney repeated it in 1900. It is the figure you will see most often.

A 1973 study that worked from the detachment records found about 2,000 deaths during the journey itself. That is lower partly because it counts a narrower period and only what officials recorded.

In 1984 the demographer Russell Thornton approached it differently. He estimated what the Cherokee population should have been without removal and compared it with what it was. He concluded deaths may have been twice the usual figure, about 8,000.

None of these is simply wrong. They answer different questions. In your capstone, name the figure you use, say where it comes from, and acknowledge the range.

Check yourself: Answer the review question on the slide in one or two sentences.

Pierian Spring · Ethnic cleansing or genocide?

Historians disagree about which word best fits Indian Removal.

"Ethnic cleansing"

Historian Gary Clayton Anderson, Ethnic Cleansing and the Indian (2014), argues that U.S. policy aimed mainly to remove Native peoples from land, so ethnic cleansing is the more accurate term for most of it.

"Genocide"

Historian Jeffrey Ostler, Surviving Genocide (2019), argues that removal policies, carried out knowing they would kill many, belong within a history of genocide that Native nations survived.

Your worksheet's definition notes that the two "can overlap." Both historians would agree the Cherokee were driven from their homeland by force.
Review question: Which part of the definition, "removal rather than complete physical destruction," matters most for deciding between the two words, and why?

Sources: Anderson, Ethnic Cleansing and the Indian: The Crime That Should Haunt America (2014); Ostler, Surviving Genocide: Native Nations and the United States from the American Revolution to Bleeding Kansas (2019).

Your capstone asks whether Indian Removal fits the definition of ethnic cleansing. Professional historians are asking a related question: is ethnic cleansing the right word, or genocide?

Gary Clayton Anderson argues that the main goal of U.S. policy was to get Native people off the land, not to kill them all, so ethnic cleansing fits better. He thinks calling it genocide can blur what actually happened.

Jeffrey Ostler argues that officials carried out removal knowing it would kill many people, and that removal belongs within a longer history of genocide that Native nations survived. His title, Surviving Genocide, puts Native survival at the center.

Notice what both agree on: the Cherokee were driven from their homeland by force, and thousands died. The debate is about how to name it.

Your worksheet's definition says the two can overlap. Use that sentence carefully in your conclusion.

Check yourself: Answer the review question on the slide in three or four sentences.

Pierian Spring · Handling sources with care

Some of the most famous Trail of Tears stories are the least reliable.

"Let him enforce it"

Jackson's famous line about John Marshall first appeared in print in 1864. His real 1832 letter said the ruling "has fell still born."

John G. Burnett, 1890

A "soldier's story" written for his 80th birthday, 52 years after the events. Some historians doubt parts of it, and its authorship has been questioned.

Quatie Ross's blanket

Quatie Ross did die near Little Rock in 1839. The story that she gave her blanket to a sick child comes from later retellings, not from records of the time.

Rebecca Neugin, 1932

A real memory, recorded 94 years later. Test it: does it match letters written in 1838, like Evan Jones's?

"Cherokee Phoenix, 1838"

The Phoenix stopped printing in 1834. A quote dated to it in 1838 needs checking before you use it.

Your rule

Ask who wrote it, when, how they knew, and whether a source from the time agrees.

Review question: Pick one document from your primary source reader and explain how close its author was to the events, in time and in place.

The Trail of Tears is surrounded by powerful stories, and some of them are shaky. Your capstone grade depends on handling sources carefully, so here are some to watch.

"John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it" first appeared in print in 1864, more than thirty years after the ruling. Jackson's real letter is better evidence.

John G. Burnett's "birthday story" of 1890 claims to be a soldier's memory of the removal. It was written 52 years later, and historians doubt parts of it. Your primary source reader includes it, so read it critically and look for support in sources from 1838.

Quatie Ross, John Ross's wife, really did die near Little Rock in 1839. The story that she gave her blanket to a sick child appears in later retellings, not in records from the time.

Rebecca Neugin's memory is real but was recorded 94 years later. It matches what Evan Jones wrote in 1838, which strengthens it.

Finally, the Cherokee Phoenix stopped publishing in 1834. If a document claims to quote it in 1838, check it before relying on it.
